interactions: Levetiracetam with dexamethasone, metformin, amlodipine or pantoprazole: no clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interaction; levetiracetam is renally cleared and neither induces nor inhibits CYP enzymes.

Lacosamide with amlodipine, metformin or pantoprazole: no clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interaction. Lacosamide prolongs the PR interval; obtain a baseline ECG and use caution with other drugs that slow AV conduction (beta-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem). Amlodipine does not prolong the PR interval.

Phenytoin, fosphenytoin, carbamazepine or phenobarbital with dexamethasone: CYP3A4 induction substantially lowers dexamethasone exposure, and dexamethasone can alter phenytoin concentrations; enzyme-inducing ASMs also lower the exposure of many anticancer drugs.
Acyclovir with metformin: no direct interaction, but acyclovir crystal nephropathy or acute kidney injury causes metformin accumulation and a risk of lactic acidosis.
Dexamethasone with metformin: corticosteroids raise blood glucose; glucose-lowering therapy may need to be intensified.

warnings: Acyclovir: give with adequate IV hydration and infuse over at least 1 hour to reduce crystal nephropathy; monitor creatinine and reduce the dose when creatinine clearance falls.

Levetiracetam: reduce the dose when creatinine clearance is below 80 mL/min; irritability or behavioral change may occur.
Valproate: hepatotoxicity, thrombocytopenia and hyperammonemia; check platelets and liver tests before use.

Treat the nonconvulsive status epilepticus under continuous EEG: IV benzodiazepine, then a non-inducing second-line IV ASM (levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, maximum 4500 mg, or lacosamide), with ICU care and escalation to an anesthetic infusion only if seizures persist.

Involve oncology in the plan and in surveillance of the treated sinonasal adenocarcinoma.

results.finding: Drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom.

general.summary: Epilepsy is diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one with a high recurrence risk, and focal seizures are classified by onset and awareness (ILAE 2014, 2017). Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is first-line monotherapy for focal seizures (NICE NG217), and drug resistance is failure of two appropriate medication schedules (ILAE 2010).

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. R is a 59-year-old right-handed man with a recent history of adenocarcinoma of the paranasal sinuses infiltrating the skull base, treated with microsurgical resection approximately 6 months ago followed by adjuvant radiochemotherapy completed 3 months ago. He was in his usual post-treatment state until approximately 10 days prior to admission when his wife noticed increasing forgetfulness and disorientation. He began misplacing items, asking repetitive questions, and on two occasions became lost within his own home. Over the following days, his confusion worsened progressively. Five days before admission, his wife observed him having episodes of staring blankly for 20-30 seconds, during which he would make chewing or lip-smacking movements and was unresponsive to verbal commands. These episodes occurred 3-4 times daily and were followed by a period of increased drowsiness lasting several minutes. He had no convulsive activity witnessed by his family. On the day of admission he was found sitting in a chair, essentially unresponsive, and was brought to the emergency department. On arrival he was somnolent but arousable, opening eyes to voice. He could state his name but was disoriented to time, place, and situation. A low-grade fever of 37.9 degrees Celsius was noted. There was concern for infectious or paraneoplastic etiology given his oncologic history. He was admitted to the neurology service for further evaluation. Since admission, the episodic staring spells with oral automatisms have continued, and the patient has had fluctuating levels of consciousness, with periods of relative alertness alternating with obtundation. Nursing staff have documented at least 8-10 such episodes per day. There is no history of prior seizures. No recent travel, sick contacts, or new medication changes. His dexamethasone had been tapered from 8 mg twice daily to 4 mg twice daily two weeks before symptom onset.

neurological_exam.additional: Intermittent episodes of behavioral arrest with oral automatisms (lip-smacking, chewing movements) lasting 10-30 seconds observed during examination. Patient appears amnestic for these episodes. No convulsive activity witnessed.
